video.title: Secrets to Making BIG Profits from Small Email Lists

summary: Koerner Office host Chris Koerner interviews Tyler Deng, co-founder of Beehive (newsletter platform, ex-Morning Brew growth lead), about monetising small email lists and growing newsletters. Topics include niche audiences monetised through cohorts, recruiting fees and events, paid acquisition and co-registration (Boost), local newsletters, content-led brand building, a referral-program 80/20 and turning a company's customer email list into a daily ad-supported newsletter. Key takeaway: niche, high-intent audiences can out-earn larger lists, and quality content plus cheap, trackable acquisition matters more than growth hacks. Both speakers have affiliate or product interests in Beehive.

speakers.name: Chris Koerner
speakers.description: Host of The Koerner Office; runs businesses such as Texas Snacks and a podcast/newsletter

speakers.name: Tyler Deng
speakers.description: Co-founder of Beehive newsletter platform, formerly ran paid acquisition at Morning Brew; writes the Big Desk Energy newsletter

ideas.name: Local newsletter sponsored by local businesses
ideas.one_liner: Hyper-local newsletter for a town or neighbourhood, monetised by sponsorships from nearby small businesses.
ideas.business_model: Sponsorships/ads sold to local businesses, with potential to extend into other revenue lines
ideas.customer: Local residents (readers) and local small businesses (advertisers)
ideas.problem: Small local businesses need customers; large newsletters cannot target geography precisely, whereas a local newsletter guarantees local readers.
ideas.offer: A local guide (restaurants, events, local news) emailed to residents, with sponsor placements for local businesses.

pricing.model: Ad/sponsorship CPMs, claimed about twice those of non-local newsletters
pricing.notes: No specific sponsorship prices given; only a relative CPM claim.

acquisition_channels.details: Facebook ads targeting residents of a specific city at roughly 50 cents per subscriber, versus about $1.50 for business subscribers.

quote.text: if I go look for Plano, Texas residents for my Plano, Texas newsletter, it's going to be about 50 cents
quote.speaker: Tyler Deng

acquisition_channels.details: Targeted postcard to every household in a handful of zip codes, estimated about $5,000 for an Annapolis-sized newsletter.
Give popular local pizza places cards to hand to customers, or run affiliate-style deals with local establishments for acquisition only.
Start with 50-75 friends and acquaintances, ask each to share with one person.

ideas.delivery: The founder writes or curates the newsletter (restaurants, events, news) and sells sponsorships; AI tools could help produce content.
unit_economics_claims: Subscriber cost about 50 cents locally versus about $1.50 for other newsletters
Postcard campaign about $5,000 for several zip codes
ideas.startup_cost: Not stated for a local newsletter; paid acquisition of a few thousand subscribers at about 50 cents each implied.
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Not stated; Tyler cites newsletters going from 100 friends to 5,000 in a quarter and selling out Q1 sponsor inventory.

acquisition.how: Paid social ads and referral programs run largely by software; postcards and partnerships need human effort. Cold DMs to businesses would risk PECR issues.

onboarding.how: Subscriber signup is automated via the platform; sponsor onboarding is a simple intake that agents can handle.

delivery.how: Agents can research local events and draft issues, but local knowledge and taste need regular human review.

billing.how: Sponsor invoicing and platform ad payments can be automated.

support.how: Mostly reader replies and sponsor queries, which agents can handle.

uk_applicability.notes: Works in UK towns and boroughs; Facebook geo-targeting works similarly. Subscriber costs differ and consent and GDPR apply to list building. Local newsletter tooling is available in the UK.

risks: Subscriber and CPM numbers are speaker estimates for the US
Local sponsor sales can be slow
Audience size is capped by local population

quotes.text: very bullish on local newsletters, and I think it makes perfect sense.
quotes.speaker: Tyler Deng

quotes.text: you can acquire subscribers for local newsletters at like half or a third of the cost of a any other newsletter.
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.name: Turn a company's customer email list into a daily ad-supported newsletter
ideas.one_liner: Agency or individual converts a business's large customer email database into a separate daily content newsletter monetised with ads and affiliates.
ideas.business_model: Agency fee or revenue share on net-new newsletter revenue (ads, sponsorships, affiliates)
ideas.customer: Ecommerce and other businesses sitting on large customer email lists
ideas.problem: Businesses use their email lists only for promotions and miss a new revenue line and brand-goodwill benefit.
ideas.offer: Create and run a topical daily newsletter on the business's list, selling ads or affiliate placements as a new revenue stream.

pricing.notes: Chris estimates revenue of about $60,000 per month from a 150,000-subscriber list; agency pricing not given.

acquisition_channels.details: Pitch directly to businesses with large email databases, with no specific method stated.

ideas.delivery: Writer or AI-assisted content team produces the newsletter and sells ads; the main difficulty is filling ad space.
unit_economics_claims: Chris: 100,000 subscribers daily could earn about $50,000 per month
Chris: 150,000 list at decent CPM could be about $60,000 per month
ideas.time_to_first_revenue: Tyler says it could bring in money from day one via ads or affiliates.

acquisition.how: B2B pitching to a few companies is mostly manual; cold email to limited companies is legal but needs personalisation.

onboarding.how: Data access and list import can be semi-automated.

delivery.how: Agents can draft daily issues with human editorial review; ad sales remain difficult.

billing.how: Invoicing and ad platform payouts are automatable.

support.how: Client queries are handled by agents with occasional human input.

uk_applicability.notes: UK PECR/GDPR require that customers consented to receive different content; repurposing a customer list for a new unrelated newsletter may need fresh opt-in. Otherwise the same.

risks: Filling ad inventory is described as the hardest part
Subscribers may not engage with a new, different newsletter
Consent and data protection when repurposing lists
Revenue figures are rough back-of-envelope estimates

quotes.text: I think there's a huge opportunity for agencies or even an individual
quotes.speaker: Tyler Deng

quotes.text: if I have 100,000 subscribers I can make $50,000 a month topline at like a a good CPM like in a business niche
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.name: Buy bankrupt company for its email list and monetise as newsletter
ideas.one_liner: Acquire asset-light bankrupt companies mainly for their email lists, then convert to daily newsletters.
ideas.business_model: Buy distressed company, monetise list through ads and promotions
ideas.customer: Email subscribers of the acquired company; advertisers
ideas.problem: Large engaged lists are undervalued in bankruptcy sales.
ideas.offer: Purchase the list cheaply and run a newsletter or ecommerce play.

price_points.label: Acquisition price of bankrupt company with 1M active emails

pricing.notes: A contact is buying a bankrupt physical-goods company with 1M active emails for about $500k.

acquisition_channels.details: Search bankruptcy filings for asset-light companies with large email lists.

ideas.delivery: Operate list as a daily newsletter and sell ads.
unit_economics_claims: Chris: could be a mid-seven-figure business if converted to a daily newsletter

acquisition.how: Screening bankruptcy filings can be tooled, but deal-making is human.

onboarding.how: Legal acquisition and data transfer need humans.

uk_applicability.notes: UK insolvency sales exist, but customer data transfer is constrained by GDPR and PECR consent, so lists often cannot be freely reused.

risks: Data protection and consent limits on reuse
Idea is speculative and not tested by Chris

quotes.text: that's like a mid7 figure business just if you converted those emails to a daily newsletter
quotes.speaker: Chris Koerner

ideas.name: Newsletter-community cohorts and recruiting placement fees (Design Buddies)
ideas.one_liner: A design community newsletter earns six figures from paid cohorts and placement fees to employers.
ideas.business_model: Paid cohorts four times a year plus recruiting placement fees plus ads
ideas.customer: Designers (cohort participants) and companies hiring designers
ideas.problem: Companies want vetted design talent; designers want training and community.
ideas.offer: Two-week design cohorts and talent placement from a vetted 10-15k community.

pricing.notes: Chris also cites 10-30% of first-year salary or $20-50k.

acquisition_channels.details: Sells to the 10-15k member newsletter community.

ideas.delivery: Run live cohorts and match designers to employers.
ideas.startup_cost: Chris: about $40-50k of paid ads to build a 10-15k list, though Tyler says it may not be needed

acquisition.how: Audience built via ads and referral flows.

delivery.how: Live cohorts and recruiting need humans.

uk_applicability.notes: Works in UK; recruitment fees are normal.

risks: Requires domain expertise and community credibility

tactics.name: Seed a newsletter with 50-75 friends then multiply via sharing
steps: Ask friends, coworkers and community members to subscribe for free
Provide real value so they stay
Ask each to share with one person to reach 150-200 quickly
Only then add paid growth

quote.text: you have a base of like 50 to 75
quote.speaker: Tyler Deng

tactics.name: Break-even paid acquisition via co-registration
steps: Recommend 3 partner newsletters in your signup flow
Spend about $2 per subscriber on Facebook or Instagram
Receive about $2 per partner subscription
Reinvest surplus into more ads

quote.text: if I'm spending $2 to acquire an email on Facebook or Instagram they come in through my flow and they subscribe to one of those three newsletters I'm break even right off the bat
quote.speaker: Tyler Deng

tactics.name: Normalise acquisition cost by engagement
steps: Tag each source with UTM parameters and segments
Compare open and click rates by source
Judge cost per engaged subscriber, not cost per signup
Dial spend up or down on the best sources

quote.text: You need to normalize it for opens.
quote.speaker: Tyler Deng

tactics.name: Advertise in other newsletters
steps: Place ads or recommendations in newsletters with similar readers
Track quality of resulting subscribers
Double down on best sources

tactics.name: One-referral reward to bootstrap referrals
steps: Create a high-value free asset (a one-page expert summary)
Offer it for just one referral
Automate delivery in the platform
Push referrers toward further tiers afterwards

quote.text: what is enticing enough to incentivize someone to share with just one person
quote.speaker: Tyler Deng

tactics.name: Test new ad channels early
steps: Try new ad formats while competition is low
Make sure you can track quality
Scale what works, stop what fails

tactics.name: Content-first brand nurturing for businesses
steps: Spend 30 minutes brainstorming what customers want more of
Publish useful content unrelated to selling
Mix in a weekly transactional email

warnings.warning: People who enter a niche without expertise or passion tend to fail.
Large multi-tier referral rewards rarely get completed; most people will not refer 5-10 people.

lessons.lesson: A small, niche, high-intent audience can earn more than a larger generic one by selling events, cohorts and placements instead of only ads.

quote.text: yet are bringing in more revenue than newsletters 10x their size
quote.speaker: Tyler Deng

lessons.lesson: Treat an audience as an asset with many possible monetisation routes; start with one and expand.
Measure acquisition quality, not just cost per signup.
Leaders should be open to testing unconventional channels, provided you can track results.
Early adoption of new ad placements gives low CPMs before the window closes.
Content-led brand building wins purchase decisions later even if it cannot be attributed directly.
Founders should have expertise or real interest in the niche they build an audience around.
Make the first referral the easiest and most rewarding step; low barriers beat large far-away rewards.
Existing business assets such as customer email lists can be repurposed into separate revenue streams.

evidence_quality.rationale: Mostly second-hand examples and back-of-envelope math; Tyler's first-hand Morning Brew experience is credible but figures are sparse and unverified. Many revenue claims are hypothetical.
evidence_quality.promotional_conflict: Tyler Deng co-founded Beehive and Chris Koerner promotes a Beehive affiliate link and his own newsletter and podcast.
